newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr down and desperate after dire data.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr down and desperate after dire data.

text.p: The Australian dollar dived 1/2 cent to 16-month lows at a hectic midsession after disastrous jobs data made another rate cut seem a dead certainty.

In defiance of all expectations employment fell 40,300 in May, the biggest monthly drop since April 1993, when the market had confidently looked for a 15,000 rise. The unemployment rate ticked up just a basis point to 8.8 percent, but only because the number of people looking for work fell sharply. Without that, unemployment would have hit 9.3 percent.
The data will force the market to question its entire upbeat view on the economy and put intense pressure on the RBA to ease.
By 12.15 pm (0215 GMT) the dollar had sunk to US$0.7505/10, its lowest level since February last year, from US$0.7564/69 just before the data hit dealing screens and US$0.7590/95 late here Wednesday.

On the crosses it had enjoyed an early bounce to 85.00 yen as US$/yen rallied but after the data it recoiled to 84.45/55, although that was still up on Wednesday's 84.10/20. In trade weighted terms it slumped to 56.8 from a previous 57.3 finish.
The latest slide brought the dollar's losses to almost three cents since the Reserve Bank last cut rates on May 23 and dealers saw further pain ahead as the market priced in another.

The September 90-day bank bill, which most accurately reflects market thinking on where official rates are heading, leapt 21 basis points to 94.87. That implied a rate of 5.13 percent compared to the present 5.50 percent cash rate.

Bond yields fell sharply and were now below those in the U.S. right out to five years. Short term interest rates were well below their U.S. equivalents meaning investors had to pay for the privilege of holding A$'s instead of U.S. dollars.
Many U.S. investors had already shown their displeasure with this novel situation -- the last time domestic rates were not above the U.S. was in the early 1980s -- by dumping the dollar.
Traders suspected the increasing prospect of another rate cut would make sellers of Japanese and European investors as well and see the dollar test 75 cent support near term.

Beneath that was a yawning gap on the charts from January 1996 when the dollar had delved as deep as 73 cents before embarking on a steady rally to 80 cents in May. Some support was expected at US$0.7450 and US$0.7380, but analysts could not rule out a return to that 73 low if the RBA did indeed ease again.
The risks certainly seemed to favour further policy action given the RBA partly justified its last four easings by pointing to the stubbornly high rate of unemployment.

The bank was bound to be disappointed, therefore, that the 150 basis points of easing delivered in the second half last year had had such a negligible effect on employment -- since the first cut in July last year the unemployment rate has actually risen to stand at 8.8 percent in May from 8.6 percent then.

Analysts said some would argue employment was a lagging indicator, but noted the media coverage of today's data was likely to have a depressant effect on consumer sentiment and spending which could turn into a vicious downward cycle.
There were no redeeming features in the breakdown of the figures, with crucial full time employment also down 23,100.

Some forward indicators, such as ANZ job advertisements, were still pointing to a pickup in employment growth later in the year but after today it would be asking a lot for the RBA to simply trust this would happen and not take out further insurance.
The political pressure for an easing was also likely to be intense with the government's budget prediction of 2.0 percent jobs growth in 1997/89 looking ever shakier.
The next RBA board meeting is on July 1, but there is no reason why the bank could not move earlier as it did with its last easing. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
